title: SYSK Selects: All We Know About Guessing
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on guessing. Josh and Chuck open with a Derek del Guadio illusion show, then discuss how the brain makes guesses (science still doesn't fully know the pathways), types of guesses (wild guess, educated guess, estimate, intuition, the military term "swag"), and how to get better at guessing through feedback and practice, including estimating jelly beans in a jar. They cover emotional guessing and empathic accuracy, cognitive distortions and polarized thinking, and how personal history colors guesses about others. Later segments cover multiple-choice test strategies from William Poundstone's book, winning at rock paper scissors using game theory, and theory of mind in apes and the false-belief test used to screen for autism. The episode closes with a listener email about registering to vote in Texas with an Alabama divorce decree.
topics: wild guess vs educated guess vs estimate

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode on guessing and the hosts chat about a Derek del Guadio illusion show and how magic relies on guessing and suggestion. Josh notes science has little firm knowledge of how guesses are made.

segments.title: Guessing in history and types of guesses
segments.summary: The hosts discuss guessing as survival in early times and Lewis and Clark's distance estimate, off by about forty miles. They then sort guesses into wild guesses, educated guesses and estimates, and introduce the military term swag, said to date to Vietnam and General Westmoreland.

segments.title: The brain and guessing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain that many brain regions are involved in guessing and that scientists cannot yet describe the full cascade. Spatial reasoning, numerical quantity and facial recognition are discussed as specialized abilities, and guesses are split into intellectual and emotional buckets.

segments.title: Intuition and getting better at guessing
segments.summary: Intuition is framed as estimation built on experience. Chuck describes improving at guessing crowd sizes through live shows. The hosts then cover the jelly bean jar method: know the container's volume, then account for packing fraction of spheres (about 64 percent) versus non-spherical items like circus peanuts (about 50 percent).

segments.title: Emotional guessing and empathic accuracy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss empathic accuracy research by Ickes and Gottman-style pioneers, and Josh shares his experience of realizing he was poor at reading others' thoughts and feelings. They discuss taking people at face value.

segments.title: Cognitive distortion and personal history
segments.summary: They discuss cognitive distortions and polarized thinking as reasons people misjudge others' feelings. Personal history and character traits color guesses, such as a liar assuming others are lying. They note that people often treat their guesses as facts.

segments.title: Guessing on multiple choice tests
segments.summary: The hosts discuss SAT and ACT guessing penalties and William Poundstone's book Rock Breaks Scissors. His tips include choosing the longest answer, the all-of-the-above and none-of-the-above myth, looking at neighboring answers, and eliminating outliers and near-duplicates, with an SAT example.

segments.title: Winning at rock paper scissors
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a Motherboard article on game theory and rock paper scissors, based on research with students at a university in China. Tips include opening with paper against men who open with rock, playing the option not played last round, and mirroring the opponent.

segments.title: Mirror neurons, theory of mind, and apes
segments.summary: Mirror neurons and theory of mind are described as ways people predict others' actions, using the apple example. Research found chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans can attribute mental states to others. The Sally-Anne false-belief test is described as a way to screen for autism in children.

segments.title: Listener mail: registering to vote in Texas
segments.summary: Monica describes moving from Alabama to Texas in 2013 and facing repeated obstacles registering to vote. A county clerk disputed her court-ordered name change from an Alabama divorce, and she was eventually registered after a supervisor intervened.
